data.text/html:
Bootstrap resampling: one sample, many universes

An interactive companion to DataMListic's video "Bootstrap Resampling - Explained".
You measured 30 trees in a forest and the average came out to 14.2 m. How sure are you about that number?
The bootstrap answers this using nothing but the sample you already have. We follow the video's chapters: one sample → the imagined multiverse → the bootstrap trick → the bootstrap distribution → standard error & CI → why it works. Color language used throughout: ■ red = the truth (population, true mean μ) · ■ purple = your one sample · ■ blue = the true sampling distribution (other universes) · ■ orange = bootstrap resamples

data.text/markdown:
1 · One sample, one number

You walk into the forest, measure ||(n = 30||) trees and compute the sample mean ||[\bar X = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i .||]That one number is all you know. If you came back tomorrow and measured 30 different trees, you would not get the same number again. The number would wiggle. The real question is: by how much? Press the button to go back to the forest and measure another 30 trees.

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eClick the button 5–10 times and write down the sample means. How far do they stray from 14?\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eNotice: in real life you only ever get \u003cstrong\u003eone\u003c/strong\u003e click. The wiggle is invisible to you.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
2 · The imagined multiverse

Imagine repeating the whole experiment in parallel universes. Each universe collects its own 30 trees and hands you a slightly different ||(\bar X||). Put all those means on a number line and they form a little cloud around the true average ||(\mu||). That cloud is the sampling distribution of ||(\bar X||), the dream object. Its width is exactly the uncertainty you want, the standard error: ||[\operatorname{SE}(\bar X) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}||]Press ▶ play and watch universes appear. Each one measures ||(n||) trees (small dots), computes its mean, and drops it onto the pile.

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ePress \u003cstrong\u003e⏩ +1000\u003c/strong\u003e. The blue cloud is centered on the red μ, and its width matches \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\sigma/\\sqrt{n}||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eChange \u003cstrong\u003en\u003c/strong\u003e to 120: the cloud gets \u003cstrong\u003ehalf\u003c/strong\u003e as wide as at n = 30 (√4 = 2). Change it to 5: wide and slightly skewed.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eThe catch:\u003c/strong\u003e you only get \u003cstrong\u003eone\u003c/strong\u003e universe. This whole picture is forever out of reach… unless you use the bootstrap.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
3 · The bootstrap trick

The magical idea: take your one sample and treat it as if it were the entire population. Then draw a new sample from it, the same size ||(n||), but with replacement. Some trees get picked twice, some get skipped, some show up three times. Formally you draw ||(X^*_1, \dots, X^*_n||) from the empirical distribution ||(\hat F_n||), which is a fancy way of saying pick uniformly from your original sample, with replacement. Each resample gives a new mean ||(\bar X^*_b||). Below are your 30 trees as cards (height in m). Press 🎲 resample: the badge shows how many times each tree was picked. Grey cards were skipped this time.

data.text/html: <marimo-ui-element object-id='ZHCJ-0' random-id='127d204c-bf76-c9db-5f72-4a51a2b4da45'><marimo-anywidget data-initial-value='{"model_id":"380e6dafe5b049acb6ec0ad612f458e4"}' data-label='null' data-model-id='"380e6dafe5b049acb6ec0ad612f458e4"'></marimo-anywidget></marimo-ui-element>
Resample to start building the pile.

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eResample a few times and count the grey cards. About \u003cstrong\u003e11 of 30\u003c/strong\u003e (≈ 36.8%) are skipped each time.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eWhy \u003cstrong\u003ewith\u003c/strong\u003e replacement? Without it you would just shuffle the same 30 trees, and \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\bar X^*||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e would always equal \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\bar X||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e. No wiggle!\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ePress \u003cstrong\u003e×100\u003c/strong\u003e a few times and watch the orange pile take shape. That pile is the next section.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4 · The bootstrap distribution

Now do it not once but B times: ||(\bar X^*_1, \bar X^*_2, \dots, \bar X^*_B||). Stack them into a histogram and something remarkable happens: this histogram, built entirely from your single sample, has almost exactly the same shape and width as the true sampling distribution you could never see. Below we cheat (we are the simulation's god): blue is the real multiverse (5,000 universes), orange is the bootstrap from one purple sample. Note the bootstrap is centered at your ||(\bar X||), not at ||(\mu||). The bootstrap gets the wiggle right; it can't fix where your sample happened to land.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eFlip \u003cstrong\u003ecenter both\u003c/strong\u003e on. The two humps nearly coincide: same shape, same width.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eClick \u003cstrong\u003enew original sample\u003c/strong\u003e several times. The orange hump \u003cem\u003eslides around\u003c/em\u003e (it follows your \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\bar X||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e), but its \u003cstrong\u003ewidth\u003c/strong\u003e stays close to blue.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet \u003cstrong\u003en = 5\u003c/strong\u003e: the bootstrap gets noisier (5 trees is a tiny window on the forest). Set \u003cstrong\u003eB = 10\u003c/strong\u003e: a ragged histogram. B is cheap, so use thousands.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
5 · Standard error & confidence interval

Once you have the bootstrap distribution, the rest is easy:
  • Standard error = standard deviation of the bootstrap means: ||(\widehat{\operatorname{SE}} = \operatorname{sd}(\bar X^*_1, \dots, \bar X^*_B)||)
  • 95% confidence interval (percentile method): throw away the bottom 2.5% and the top 2.5% of bootstrap means. What's left is your interval: ||(\big[\, q_{0.025}(\bar X^*),\; q_{0.975}(\bar X^*) \,\big]||)
No normal assumption, no z-scores, no formulas. And it works for any statistic: try the median, which has no simple SE formula.

Does a 95% interval really catch μ 95% of the time? Let's check in the multiverse: each universe draws its own 30 trees, builds its own bootstrap CI, and we count how often it contains the true ||(\mu = 14||).

data.text/html: <marimo-ui-element object-id='xXTn-0' random-id='089fe531-fdd0-7aae-26c7-452223076a66'><marimo-button data-initial-value='0' data-label='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e🌌 Run 300 universes (B = 1000 each)\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"neutral"' data-disabled='false' data-full-width='false'></marimo-button></marimo-ui-element>

data.text/markdown: Press the button to run the coverage experiment.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSlide the level from 95 to 50: the grey tails grow, the interval shrinks. Then rerun coverage: about half the intervals miss.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSwitch the statistic to \u003cstrong\u003emedian\u003c/strong\u003e or \u003cstrong\u003e90th percentile\u003c/strong\u003e: the same two lines of code give you an SE and a CI, and no formula is needed.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eFor the \u003cstrong\u003emean\u003c/strong\u003e, compare the percentile CI to the textbook \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\bar X \\pm 1.96\\,s/\\sqrt n||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e. They nearly agree, a good sanity check.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
6 · Why it works: the empirical distribution

Why on earth should resampling from your own data mimic new draws from the forest? Because of the empirical CDF ||[\hat F_n(x) = \frac{1}{n}\,\#\{\,i : X_i \le x\,\}.||]With 10 data points ||(\hat F_n||) is a jagged staircase barely resembling the truth. With 100 it tightens up, and with 1,000 it's almost indistinguishable from the real ||(F||). Resampling from the data is sampling from ||(\hat F_n||), so if ||(\hat F_n \approx F||), bootstrap resamples behave like fresh samples from the forest.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eStep n from 10 → 100 → 1000. The staircase hugs the red curve, and the gap shrinks like \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(1/\\sqrt n||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e (Glivenko–Cantelli / DKW).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eAt n = 10, resample a few times: the staircase is wildly different each time. That's why bootstrap with tiny samples is shaky.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eLimits:\u003c/strong\u003e the bootstrap struggles with extremes (e.g. the \u003cem\u003emaximum\u003c/em\u003e: a resample can never exceed your tallest tree) and with dependent data (time series need block bootstrap).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
7 · Sandbox: bootstrap your own data

Your sample is now a set of draggable trees on a number line. Drag a point, double-click empty space to add one, double-click a point to remove it. While you drag, the purple line (||(\bar X||)) and median follow instantly in JS. On release, Python bootstraps your data and draws the orange bootstrap distribution with its CI.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eChallenges\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ePress \u003cstrong\u003eAdd an outlier 🌳\u003c/strong\u003e. Which statistic's CI blows up more, \u003cstrong\u003emean\u003c/strong\u003e or \u003cstrong\u003emedian\u003c/strong\u003e? (Robustness, visible.)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eChoose \u003cstrong\u003emax\u003c/strong\u003e. The bootstrap histogram piles up on your tallest tree and can never go higher. This is a known bootstrap failure.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eUse \u003cstrong\u003eTiny (n=4)\u003c/strong\u003e with \u003cstrong\u003emedian\u003c/strong\u003e: count the distinct values. A 4-point sample has only a handful of possible resamples, so the \"distribution\" is a few spikes.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eLoad \u003cstrong\u003eTwo clumps\u003c/strong\u003e and look at the mean: the bootstrap reveals a lumpy, non-normal sampling distribution that a ±1.96·SE formula would hide.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

"Your sample, as small and humble as it looks, is actually the best window you have onto the population."
